contact_edits.before: The style's side effects include recurrent outbreaks of whiny or rhetorical acting. In Eda Holmes' production, only two actors are immune. One is Juan Chioran, who as the painter is required to speak Italian and to sing, both of which he does with great melodiousness, but who is equally cool and commanding when talking in English. The other, in a tougher part and with less experience to draw on, is Marc Bendavid whose troubled, passionate naivete as the priest is the evening's driving force, He doesn't bring off the end when, having suffered a dire transformation, he has to persuade us that something has actually happened, but I doubt if anyone could. The normally luminous Jenny Young is bafflingly uneven as Mary of the Secrets, sometimes in command, sometimes just shouting. As the physician, Brian Dooley hardly gets beyond gruff rudeness, though I think he's meant to be a cynical teller of unwelcome truths. Nicola Correia-Damude begins arrestingly as Mary of the Sheets, but then finds nowhere to go; ditto Miranda Edwards' Mary Frances who gets very sulky. As the deluded Mary Anne, a key role judging from her position in the curtain call, Shannon Taylor has some piercing moments but mostly picks her way through her words as if they were a minefield. If I haven't engaged with the play's deeper themes (faith, art, etc.) that's because I can't detect where they are. And to be honest, I don't care. - The Madonna Painter runs until Dec. 13. Call 416-504-4060 or visit factorytheatre.cafor tickets and information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com
